subject: fabergeEgg
pitch:
Category: Object.
Subject: jewelled egg opening to reveal a tiny automaton.
Style: Fabergé enamel and gold.
reasoning:
I'm planning a single TypeScript module for a jewelled Fabergé egg that opens to reveal a tiny automaton, sized realistically at roughly 8-10 cm tall with a gold stand bringing the total to about 0.15 m, with a hinge joint for the lid opening.

Now I'm thinking through the construction: a lathed gold stand with scrolled feet and an enamel band supporting the egg, while the egg itself is modeled as hollow shells (outer and inner walls) split into a lower body and an upper lid so the interior automaton is visible. The lid attaches via a hinge joint at the back rim and rotates open roughly 100-110 degrees backward, and I'm working out the exact rotation axis and bone orientation so the lid tilts correctly without ambiguity.

Working through the rotated rim center, I find the lid's concave interior ends up facing forward-up, which confirms the lid has fallen back with its opening tilted toward the viewer correctly.

I'll go with -100° instead, so the lid stands upright at the back with its interior facing forward, blocking nothing from the front view.

Now I need the egg itself to show an opening — cutting the lower shell above the equator so the automaton inside becomes visible, based on the egg's overall height and equator width.

Working out the egg's profile with an asymmetric radius function (narrower at the top for the pointy end), then positioning the egg's center height relative to the stand's top ring so it sits correctly in the base.

I'm placing the cut line slightly above the equator to split the shell into a shorter, taller lid and a longer lower shell, each lathed from radius/height profiles with a thin wall thickness defined by inner and outer curve outlines.

Now I'm thinking through the paint treatment — wanting a custom enamel guilloché pattern, considering a deep translucent color like royal blue or red for the egg's surface finish.

Adding equator bands, then I'll bring in the clockwork kit for metal gilt materials and gear trains to place beneath the automaton's platform, plus glow effects for jewels.

For the automaton itself, I'm imagining a tiny gold-and-enamel ballerina figure: a pale pink ruffled skirt lathed as a cone, torso, head with a painted face decal, outstretched arms, hair in a bun, and one leg raised en pointe, standing around 4.5cm tall inside the egg's cavity.

I'm working out where to cut the lower shell higher up so the bowl is shallower, and placing a small gold platform disk inside at a height where the ballerina rises up out of the bowl with her head clearing the cut line.

I'm now thinking about adding tiny flat gears around the figure's base on the platform top as a visible mechanism, considering a stepped gold pedestal to keep the figure from feeling cramped alongside the gear train.

I'm figuring out the lid hinge joint placement and rotation axis, reasoning through how positive degrees should tip the bone to match the lid's swing direction, landing on a -100 degree pose for that hinge.

Going forward, I'll build the lid's geometry at its closed position first using absolute model coordinates, then apply the pose transform afterward, since paint and part placement get evaluated at build time. Next I'm sketching out the automaton's joint hierarchy: a turntable at the base, then a chain of doll joints (hip, spine, neck, head) plus arm chains for the ballerina figure, each assigned appropriate roles.

I'm also considering adding a small winding key detail on the base, possibly rigged with its own rotation joint, though I want to keep the rig moderate and avoid over-engineering it—just one root joint with clear chain parenting. Then I'm planning the decorative jewelwork: cabochon gems set in gold collets around the rim and lid in a floral pattern, pearls, and gold filigree meridian bands.

For the lid, I'm designing a finial topped with a crowned cabochon gem and pearl, plus a painted sunburst enamel interior lining using radial rays in pale blue and silver. The exterior shell gets a translucent royal blue guilloché enamel with lighter sunburst waves, gold rim bands, and a matching lower shell pattern.

For textures, I'm aiming for 5-8 total, including a ballerina face decal with painted eyes and rosy cheeks, and an oval enamel miniature portrait on the lid front as a nod to Fabergé's signature "surprise" eggs.

I'm settling on a laurel wreath with a central rose and pearl detailing rather than a specific monogram, keeping the decoration generically ornate. I'm also planning a gold filigree acanthus scroll decal to wrap around the lid in four sections, applied as surface decals onto the lid mesh.

For the rest, I'm adding a tiny enamel-style clock face with roman numerals onto the front of the stand's column, built as a custom SVG rather than a plain gauge texture. I'm also layering a ballerina tutu effect using stacked discs with scalloped petal-textured cards around the waist, then finishing details with merged pearl spheres, a crimson velvet noise paint for the cushion, and enamel painted accents.

Now I'm counting materials and parts to stay under the limits—aiming for roughly 300 parts total, which means I need a merging helper for grouped elements like pearls so individual beads don't blow the budget, while keeping bone-relative placement intact for posing.

I'll use mergeGeometries from three.js's BufferGeometryUtils to combine spheres and cones that share the same vertex attributes, then start laying out the actual egg geometry constants—height, equator radius, center offset, and the stand's base position.

Now I'm sketching the pedestal profile as a lathe curve, plotting (radius, height) points to shape the foot, baluster, and cup that cradles the egg's rounded bottom, sizing the cup rim radius to match the egg's curvature at that height.

Checking that the egg radius at that height roughly matches the cup's inner radius so the egg sits snugly without clipping through the cup walls.

Now I'm thinking about adding feet to the base—maybe four small gold lion-paw feet for the stand.

Instead I'll replace them with three curved gold "S" scroll brackets spaced at 90°, 210°, and 330° around the azimuth, sweeping from the foot up to the cup. I'll also add a turquoise enamel ring with pearls as a separate band on the foot disc, then move on to considering whether a clock belongs on the stand—deciding the stand is too short for that and reworking the design instead.

Now I'm shaping the pedestal with a drum section to hold a clock face decal on the front, defining the radius and height for the drum cylinder and positioning the decal with specific size and direction coordinates. I'm working out the full pedestal profile from foot to neck to drum to cup, setting the narrowing radii at each height level, and sketching out the cup's bowl curvature where it meets the egg shape inside.

Still working out the lathe profile coordinates...

Checking the egg radius at the lip height against the inner lip radius, I find the egg actually pokes slightly past the cup lip at the top—meaning the two surfaces intersect there, so I need to account for that overlap in visibility.

The intersection discrepancy is small enough to ignore, so I'll settle on the lip profile with the top edge and inner taper as close enough. For the lathe geometry, I'll go with faceted segments rather than smoothing—16 segments for finer parts and 20 for the pedestal.

For shading, I'm treating sharper corners (over 35°) as creased edges. For the pedestal, I'm going with gilt gold metal, and handling the drum as a separate part with a clock face decal placed over the gold surface using the bezel ring from the svg design.

Now I'm working out the egg radius formula, defining it based on normalized height along the egg's axis with a taper factor to shape the curve.

I'm sampling points along the egg's lower profile using discrete steps in t, starting from the bottom tip where the radius is zero, and converting these into coordinates relative to the pedestal's position for the outer shell outline.

For the inner wall, I'm trying to figure out the simplest approach: either scaling the outer radius inward by the shell thickness at each sampled point, or offsetting the y-coordinates slightly at the rim and bottom, to produce a consistent inner shell shape that mirrors the outer one.

So I'll define the inner sample using t'=tc/k so the scaled point matches the rim's y-level exactly, then build the lid shell by tracing the outer profile from tc to the top, dropping to the scaled inner top point, and running the inner profile back down to meet the rim seam at the outer starting point.

For distinguishing inner versus outer paint surfaces, I'm comparing each point's normal against the radial direction from the egg's center — if the dot product is negative, it's an interior-facing surface.

Now I'm designing the enamel paint function: interior surfaces get pale ivory or blue-grey silk tones, while the exterior gets a cobalt guilloché pattern with concentric wave bands using sine functions on the angle and height coordinates.

I'm also thinking through raised gold meridian bands—instead of relying purely on painted stripes, I'll build actual geometry sweeps along the egg's curved profile at several azimuth angles, using analytically computed offset points to form the raised bands cheaply.

I'll put a medallion on the lid front too, with a finial and gem flower motifs, and plan gilt meridian bands as flat gold box-section sweeps lifted slightly off the surface to avoid clipping. I also want gold rim bands as closed circular sweeps at the equator, on both lid and lower halves, paired with pearls around the rim.

For the lower shell I'm considering a scalloped gold calyx collar where it meets the cup, though I may just rely on the cup lip instead to keep things simple. For the lid's finial, I'm planning a gold lathe collar topped with a faceted ruby cabochon, using a geometry like an octahedron to fake a jewel cut.

For the brilliant-cut gem itself, I'm designing a lathe profile with crown and pavilion facets using a small segment count for sharpness, wrapped in a reusable gem helper that places flat-shaded gemstones with a collet ring onto a surface, using surface normal approximation to orient them correctly.

Instead of re-querying the surface after posing, I'll compute the orientation analytically: deriving the outward normal from the tangent of the egg profile curve at each point, so gems sit correctly oriented without expensive recomputation.

Now I'm sketching the lid's decoration layout — a gold band at the rim, then a ring of alternating gem motifs (ruby/emerald or ruby/diamond) spaced around several meridian angles near the lid's midline.

I'm placing six rosette flowers evenly around the lid at t=0.5, each with a central cabochon (ruby or emerald alternating) surrounded by a ring of six small pearl petals, then adding a secondary ring of small turquoise cabochons near t=0.72–0.78.

For the top, I'm designing a lathe-turned gold cap with a large faceted gem finial and four tiny pearls, plus a sunburst-patterned painted interior for the lid using alternating ivory and pale gold-bordered radial segments.

I considered trying a decal to add a gold star inside the lid, but projecting a decal onto a concave inner surface is risky given ambiguity in which surface the ray would hit, so I'll skip the decal and just rely on the painted sunburst instead.

Working through the geometry, I realize the flat disc at the apex would actually poke through the shell's curved surface near its edges since the dome drops about 3.4mm at that radius while the shell thickness is only around 3mm — so the medallion placement risks becoming visible/incorrect from outside rather than sitting flush inside the cavity.

Given that complication, I'll abandon the disc medallion idea and instead go with a painted sunburst motif plus gold ring details for the lid's decoration, and line the lid's interior with ivory silk paint featuring radial pleats for a refined finish.

For the lower shell, I'm also lining the interior with pale cream silk visible beneath the ballerina's platform, then working out the geometry for a tiny gold turntable disc the ballerina automaton stands on, calculating radii and vertical offsets so it fits properly within the inner shell curvature.

Now I'm laying out a ring of small gears around the upper tier, placing them at radius ~0.024 with module 0.0009 and 12 teeth each, working out a train of four gears positioned around the center while keeping everything within a 0.03 radius so they don't overlap.

I'm figuring out gear thickness and vertical placement so the train doesn't clip through the tutu, then deciding to split the gears into two trains—one with three gears on one side, one with two on the other—using a shared placement function with a sign flip for left versus right.

Now I'm working through the geometry for the second gear's angle, checking that its tip radius stays within the outer tier boundary, and testing angles toward +z instead of -z to keep it from poking outside the allowed radius.

I'm simplifying to two mirrored three-gear trains, where each chain builds gear1 off gear0's default position and gear2 off gear1, and I need to carefully verify there's no accidental overlap between non-meshing gears like gear0 and gear2, since the gearTrain function throws an error in that case.

Working through the geometry, I set gear0 at 18 teeth, gear1 at 10 teeth placed at a 20° angle, and gear2 at 14 teeth placed at 100° from gear1, then compute their absolute positions and confirm the distance between gear0 and gear2 clears their combined outer radii by about 1.7mm, so this layout is safe. Now I just need to pick an absolute placement for gear0 so the whole train fits within the model.

Checking a few candidate positions, I find the gears end up too close to the dancer's tutu or past the tier edge, so I rescale the whole module down by a factor of 7/9 to shrink all three gears and their separations, then recompute the relative positions for gear1 and gear2 under this smaller scale.

Checking the overlap again, that still pushes slightly past the tier boundary, so I shift the starting point further left—now g1 and g2 both fit comfortably within the .033 radius limit.

For the mirrored train, I'm placing it symmetrically at negative x, positive z, and rotating both angle offsets by 180° so the geometry matches the original train's spacing exactly.

I'll keep both gear trains using the same tooth module but could vary tooth counts for variety, and I'm checking the hub-to-rim clearance to confirm there's enough room for spokes if I want them.

For the overall rig, I'm planning six gear parts plus six arbor pins, then setting up the joint hierarchy: a static platform under base, a rotating turntable joint, and spin joints for each gear named with a consistent prefix. I'm also working out the dancer figure's hip height relative to the turntable's top surface.

Now I'm figuring out the ballerina's rest pose in a standing-en-pointe stance with arms extended and legs close together, and computing the leg segment heights (foot, ankle, knee) starting from where the feet meet the turntable surface.

I'm then stacking the hip, torso, neck, and oversized stylized head on top of the legs, placing the tutu around the hip and a bun on top, and checking that the total figure height fits under the egg's open lid line without colliding with the rim when closed.

For the rig, I'm setting up a hip joint on the turntable with a spine chain curving from hip through mid-torso to the neck, then attaching a head joint at the top—skipping a separate jaw since this is a doll figure, not a creature with a mouth.

Mouth gets painted on, so I skip joint logic there. For the arms, each side gets a three-joint chain from shoulder to elbow to wrist curving outward and slightly down for that rounded ballet-arm look, parented to the final spine joint, mirrored by sign for left versus right.

For the legs, I'm setting up a four-joint chain per side from hip to knee to ankle to toe tip, built as a catmull path with thin tube radii for straight vertical legs. Then I'm layering the tutu as three stacked pale pink lathe discs.

Writing skirt profile points...

I'm now thinking about adding a tulle ruffle effect around the waist using a ring of card elements with outward-facing frames, though I'm weighing whether that approach would actually render visibly versus using stacked lathe discs with scalloped edges instead for the tutu shape.

With lean around 60-90 degrees, the cards fan outward and downward like petals, sized small and tinted pale pink across two rings at varying radii. For the bodice, I'll sweep the torso along the spine with tapering radii in gold/pink enamel, add a collar necklace, sweep the arms in ivory skin tone, and place small sphere hands at the wrists.

For the head, I'm adding a flattened sphere with dark brown hair (cap plus bun), a gold tiara ring with a tiny ruby, and a face decal with simple eyes, blush, and mouth positioned on the front of the head sphere. All these parts stay rigid on their bones, and I'm now thinking about setting up the turntable animation.

I'm placing a gold winding key inserted into the side of the pedestal drum, with a shaft extending outward and a cloverleaf-shaped bow extruded to face the right direction, hinged for rotation.

Now I'm adding ornate pedestal legs with gold S-scroll brackets, a turquoise guilloche enamel band around the foot ring, and a pearl bead row at the base. I'm also planning a small oval medallion decal on the lower shell's front, framed in a gold ellipse with pearls and cardinal diamonds.

Working out the ellipse frame math, computing tangent-plane axes at the surface point and parameterizing the oval boundary by angle, then projecting each point back onto the egg's curved surface so the frame hugs the shell properly.

I'll build helper functions for sampling the egg surface and height-to-parameter mapping, sweep a closed Catmull-Rom path through the computed oval points with a thin gold tube and pearl accents around it, then set up gem and collet placement functions for faceted stones mounted in gold cups, plus a guilloché-style enamel finish on the pedestal base.

For the foot I'm adding a separate turquoise enamel ring at the base with its own guilloche pattern, keeping the color palette tight since metal paints don't count against the limit. I'm applying selective glow to the gemstones—moderate strength on rubies, lighter on sapphires and emeralds—while leaving diamonds unlit so they stay crisp and white rather than flat-colored.

Now I'm thinking through how to merge all the pearl beads efficiently by bucketing their positions by bone and color into a map, then flushing each group into a single merged geometry part at the end rather than building thousands of tiny individual parts. The tricky part is timing relative to posing—parts built before the pose get rotated correctly with the joint, but I need to figure out whether flushing after the pose would double-apply the bone's rotation to geometry that's already in model space.

Since the SDK converts model-space geometry to bone-local coordinates using the current (posed) inverse transform at build time, anything built in model space before the pose will land correctly once the pose is applied—so all the lid pearl work and the flush must happen before the pose call. For the hinge itself, I'm planning a gold barrel along the back edge made of rod segments: two knuckle pieces fixed to the base shell flanking a center knuckle attached to the lid, plus small gold plate details, positioned along the hinge axis.

I'm placing the hinge joint slightly outside the shell radius so the barrel sits naturally, and sketching the joint hierarchy—base as root, with lidHinge, platform, turntable, and windingKey as children with various roles. I'm also starting to define the paint/material palette, distinguishing a gilt gold for rims and bands from a brassier gold for the pedestal.

Now I'm thinking through a richer multi-tone gold scheme, adding a green-gold or rose-gold variant for decorative leaves, and planning a laurel garland on the lid using small extruded leaf shapes arranged in rosettes around the surface. Writing leaf extrusion helper...

I'm defining a small leaf outline shape with a thin extrusion thickness and a slight lift offset, using a green-gold color, and checking that such tiny extruded geometry will still render correctly as the part count keeps increasing.

Now I'm tallying up pieces roughly by assembly section: the pedestal with its lathe body, legs, enamel foot ring, decal, pearls, and three-part key totaling around eleven parts; the lower shell with its lathe body, meridian bands, rim ring, hinge pieces, decal frame, gems, and an extra gold ring near the collar bringing it to about thirty; and now I'm starting to count the lid's lathe body, bands, and rim ring in the same way.

Thinking through the lid rosettes and gem rows, I'm deciding to merge gems by color into combined geometry rather than keeping every stone separate, which keeps the glowing ruby effect intact while trimming part counts well below the 180-340 target range. I'm reasoning that part-count targets aren't a hard requirement, so I'll keep pearls merged for simplicity but leave individual gems, collets, gears, and filigree details separate where it adds meaningful richness to the automaton and pedestal.

Now I'm placing gold filigree scroll decals in the gaps between the lower shell's bands, at specific angular positions, using tinted gold SVG strokes with darker outlines, and considering whether to add similar scroll accents on the lid between the rosettes. I'm also thinking about adding a crowned monogram decal to the front of the lid.

Deciding instead to keep the lid front with a ruby rosette rather than a monogram, and settling on placing rosettes at all six gap positions on the lid rather than mixing in sprigs or a second decorative ring. I'm now cataloging the texture types I'll need: face, clock, miniature, filigree, and others.

I'll skip the extra sparkle and vignette details — five textures plus maybe a peacock-feather accent feels sufficient. Time to move on to managing overall complexity.

I need to write the code carefully to avoid runtime errors since I can't test it, paying special attention to risky APIs like decal, lathe, extrude, gear train, chain, and card/ring/pose functions. For the lathe calls, I'm thinking through the outline points, sharpness/smoothing defaults, and segment counts to get a clean faceted egg shape.

Writing the shell outline generator...

Checking the rim closure between outer and inner loops, making sure duplicate points at the axis don't cause degenerate zero-radius issues, and verifying the point count stays within the lathe geometry's 512-point limit.

Lid loop closes correctly with tc/K giving about 0.266, and the shell thickness at the equator works out to roughly 2.6mm. Now I'm writing the paint function for the enamel coating, checking whether each point is on the inside surface using the normal and center-y offset, then applying different colors based on that and the latitude angle.

Still writing enamel shader...

Simplifying the platform to gilt brass, keeping the velvet cushion silk-lined. For the ballerina I'm picking colors for skin, hair, pink bodice with gold trim, tutu countershading, ruby tiara, and ribboned pointe shoes, then sketching a small face decal with eyes, blush, mouth, and brows on a tiny sphere head.

Positioning the head joint above the neck and placing the face decal just forward of the sphere's surface, sized to fit the head, with the sphere itself slightly flattened via scale to feel more natural.

For the hair, I'm thinking of using a partial sphere cap larger than the head, offset upward and backward so it covers the crown without obscuring the face -- I need to limit the theta/phi range so it doesn't wrap all the way around to the front.

Still positioning hair geometry... adding a back hair mass, a bun sphere at the crown, and a small gold tiara made from a partial torus arc across the forehead.

For the tutu I'm placing the hip joint bone with a gold waist belt, then building the bodice as a sweep along a spine chain made from catmull points running from hip to bust to shoulders, using a varying radius that narrows at the waist and widens again at the bust and shoulders.

Now I'm adding a short skin-colored neck cylinder connecting shoulder to head, then laying out the arm skeleton with shoulder, elbow, wrist, and hand points positioned symmetrically on both sides.

Still working out leg joint positions...

Now I'm sketching the pointe shoe with a pink satin color and ribbon wrap at the ankle, and checking that the tutu rim lines up with the hip height so the legs show properly below it. Then I'm setting up the joint hierarchy, defining the hip joint parented to the turntable before building the spine chain off it.

Actually I'll simplify by skipping a separate hip joint—using the spine's first joint as the hip itself, with legs and arms parented off the spine chain accordingly. I'm also adding a short neck joint between the spine and head to position things more naturally at the shoulders.

For the spine chain with four control points there'd be three spans giving three joints named sequentially with the "spine" role, and I'm noting the rig needs a single unparented root joint at the base. The turntable joint sits at a fixed height with legs resting on its top disc, and the disc itself is a small lathed shape with a dark rim—keeping the turntable's rest pose neutral for now while figuring out how the platform part attaches.

I'm working out the gear train placement on the platform tier, calculating gear thickness from the module size and positioning the gear center just above the platform surface, then computing the mirrored second gear train's position and angle offsets using trigonometry to find the x/z coordinates in the local frame.

I'm confirming that with axis Y and up Z, the aim quaternion resolves to identity, so the local x,z coordinates map directly to model x,z, and verifying the two gear trains are positioned symmetrically on opposite sides of the dancer.

Checking the second train's gear positions by propagating the chain geometry step by step, and confirming the non-meshing gear pair satisfies the distance threshold against the sum of outer radii.

Setting up each gear's tooth count, spoke count, bore size, and angle offset, with arbor radius derived as the smaller of bore or scaled hub size, and leaning toward metallic gold/copper/blued color choices for the train.

I'm normalizing the color input so a single paint or an array both resolve into a consistent array format for the gear's fill.

Now I'm sketching the pedestal's scroll bracket legs, placing three at 120-degree intervals and plotting a curved path of radial and height points for each one.

Working out the bracket's radial path coordinates so it attaches at the foot rim, curves up and inward to connect to the drum cup, and ends with a small decorative curl, checking that it clears the drum's radius.

I'm placing the brackets at three positions around the clock (60°, 180°, 300°) so the front stays unobstructed, then positioning the winding key near the +x axis with a shaft extending outward from its joint.

Then I'm extruding a quatrefoil bow shape on the key with a flat plane facing outward and adding a ruby cabochon at its center, before working out how to apply the clock face decal onto the curved drum front while accounting for the surface curvature near the decal's edges.

I'm plotting out the pedestal's lathe profile point by point, tracing the outer silhouette from the base foot up through the stem and drum section, making sure the path doesn't self-intersect as it curves outward and back.

Now I'm checking that the inner cup wall stays properly offset from the outer wall at matching heights, verifying gaps of several millimeters to keep the walls thick enough, then confirming the egg shape nests correctly inside the bowl without clipping through the inner surface.

Adding the finial brings total height to about .176. Now I need to figure out how the lid opening affects the silhouette — rotating it roughly 100° around its hinge would swing the finial backward and tilt it upward, changing the overall height profile.

That gives a total height near 0.2 meters, which works well. With the lid standing up at the back, dome pointing back and slightly down, its interior opening faces forward and upward — a nice backdrop for the egg and dancer, with the pedestal still resting cleanly at y=0.

I'm working out the rim position where the lid cuts across the egg, computing the cut height and radius at that point so the gap between lid and shell stays around 1.4mm after rotation. Then I'm checking the dancer's head height against that cut line to make sure the figure fits properly within the open egg without poking through the rim.

Now I'm writing the egg surface function that computes points along its curve with an outward normal offset, defining the radius and height profiles then deriving a normal vector to place features correctly on the egg exterior.

Writing egg surface math...

Writing meridian band sweep code...

I'll just go with a cheap round cross-section, 6 sides at a small radius, slightly embedded for the bands. Then I'm planning the t-ranges splitting lower and lid bands around the convergence point near the finial, plus defining closed ring paths at specific azimuth points for the gold trim rings on both rim and lid.

I'm laying out where pearls go: 24 around the lid rim, 24 around the lower rim, plus foot row, mini frame, and lid rosette pearls, all added into spatial bins per bone part. Now I'm sketching out a gem-cutting helper using a lathe geometry with faceted profile points.

Adjusting gem placement offset...

For the bezel I'll orient the torus along the z-axis to seat it properly around each gem. Then for the flower rosette, I'm working out the math to place six pearl petals in a ring around a central gem, projecting their positions onto the egg's curved surface by converting the circular offset into corresponding t and degree adjustments.

For the leaves, I'm deciding to add six per rosette angled outward at 30° offsets, giving 36 leaf parts total across all rosettes — within budget, so I'll keep that count rather than trimming to four or five.

Still working out leaf extrusion and orientation...

Adjusting the collar radius calculations to better fit the egg curvature near the apex, I'm settling on placing the collar base around y=0.1595 and refining the profile points so the ruby sphere sits cleanly on top.

I'm planning four tiny diamonds around the collar, then thinking through the lower shell's calyx design—adding eight gold acanthus leaves flaring up from the cup junction to anchor the piece visually.

Switching the leaf tone to a green-gold hue for that authentic Fabergé feel, with the bottom set sized larger than the lid rosette. Bringing the total ornamental leaf count to 44, plus I'm sketching a miniature oval decoration on the lower shell's front face near the platform level.

I'm positioning a pearl ring with diamond accents around that oval frame, then spacing filigree sprigs symmetrically around the shell while checking the angular gaps stay wide enough to avoid overlap with the miniature's span.

I'm sketching a gold scroll-sprig SVG motif with a curling stem and spiral leaves, using a darker outline stroke beneath a lighter gold fill so it reads clearly at the raster scale, and weighing whether to echo this filigree on the lid as well.

Now I'm designing the clock face texture with an ivory dial, gold bezel, roman numerals, and hands fixed at 10:10, plus a miniature oval portrait decal with a pale sky-blue ground, a wreath of green leaves and pink rose roses, a ribbon bow, and a thin gold rim, clipped to transparency outside the oval. Then I move on to a plain face texture and start a scalloped petal-card texture.

For the card system, I'm planning to use light grey base fills with grey strokes so the `color` prop can tint them pink while keeping the shading neutral, and I'm working out how the ring layout attaches cards to a frame — deciding whether to pass an explicit bone reference so the cards rigidly follow the hip joint rather than defaulting to whichever joint is nearest.

I'm also figuring out the orientation for ring items: cards face outward along the ring's normal axis, lean downward with a flattened flow vector so they drape like petals, and are double-sided so both faces show. Then I'm setting up two staggered rings at slightly different radii, heights, and card sizes to create a layered skirt effect.

Now I'm tinting the tulle in pale pink tones and moving on to small hair accents. For the dancer's bodice I'm adding a thin gold trim ring around the chest, plus simple sphere hands, pointed shoes, and small flattened torus shapes at the ankles to suggest ribbon wraps, keeping jewelry details minimal.

Part count stays modest at around 35, so I'm considering a touch of whimsy to match the "magic" theme—five tiny glowing four-point star shapes floating near the dancer's head, extruded thin and subtly lit in pale gold, rigidly attached so they turn with the piece on the turntable.

Now I'm moving on to the egg's interior details: a velvet pad inside the lid, enamel paint on the lid using a shared enamel function, and a base disc with pearls plus a blue enamel foot ring. I'm thinking through simplifying the foot ring geometry by applying the enamel band directly via paint on the pedestal rather than lathing a separate ring piece.

Writing enamel paint logic...

I'm interpolating the pedestal's surface profile to find the correct height at that radius, then positioning each pearl just slightly above the surface so it reads as sitting on top rather than embedded.

No floor shadow needed, and the triangle budget seems reasonable. I'm naming the piece "Fabergé Surprise Egg" and setting up the imports, pulling in the core builder utilities plus the clockwork and glow kits separately from the main SDK package.

Checking which helpers like DEG, mix, smoothstep, and outline point types are exported from where -- I'll skip strict typing on the outline arrays and just infer coordinate tuples to keep things simple at runtime even if type-checking is loose.

Setting up the egg's dimensions and radius-profile function, then defining the metallic palettes for gilt, brass, and copper finishes...

Still writing gem colors and blend helpers...

Writing enamel shading logic...

Still writing paint functions...

I'm checking that the pedestal lathe profile uses y directly as the sample height, mapping the wall boundaries against the guilloche pattern's teal and blue zones. I need to verify the guilloche wavelength is fine enough relative to the circumference to render properly at typical paint sampling density.

Checking texel density and painted surface area to confirm the guilloche period will render cleanly without aliasing—decided to keep most dancer parts as flat colors except the tutu. Now moving on to writing the clock face SVG...

Still writing SVG code...
